title: When ICE Comes for a MAGA Supporter
summary: Last year, the conservative evangelical blogger Samuel Sey published an article on his blog, Slow to Write, defending the Trump administration’s plan for mass deportations from a Christian perspective. “Christian ethics do not denounce deportations,” he wrote. “They demand it.” Born in Ghana and a r...
content:
Last year, the conservative evangelical blogger Samuel Sey published an article on his blog, Slow to Write, defending the Trump administration’s plan for mass deportations from a Christian perspective. “Christian ethics do not denounce deportations,” he wrote. “They demand it.” Born in Ghana and a resident of Canada before he moved to the United States, Sey went on to write that “America doesn’t owe anything to people born outside of the country—including me.”

Last week, on October 21, ICE arrested Sey, who now faces deportation from the United States––a devastating blow to his American-born wife and three American children. A DHS spokesperson called Sey “an illegal alien” in a statement to news outlets. A statement attributed to Sey’s wife asserts that he entered the U.S. legally “and has been working ever since in good faith with a lawyer to obtain permanent legal status.” Some of his supporters have blamed his arrest on a clerical error. (The DHS spokesperson claimed in the statement that the 39-year-old Sey overstayed his legal entry by four years.)

Arrests of this sort are nothing new in most respects. Federal-enforcement efforts in the United States’ interior have recently averaged 19,000 deportations a month. Although some deportees are doubtless unsympathetic criminals, many thousands are good people with families or friends who suffer their absence acutely. Sey is unusual, however, in being known personally to many prominent MAGA-aligned Christians, some of whom have backed a fundraiser for his family and affirmed his good character. That support has angered some within the MAGA coalition. A prevailing MAGA narrative is Illegal immigrants are members of a lawless, untrustworthy out-group that is justly hated for the significant harm that it does to America. That narrative is threatened when a member of the MAGA in-group, whose personal and professional life many MAGA allies affirmed as good for America, is accused of being an “illegal alien.”

Perhaps that’s why the debate about Sey’s arrest has been so polarizing, and why MAGA participants are finding it harder than usual to ignore the complexities of the issue and the fissures in their coalition.

Joel Berry, who has described himself as “a right-wing protestant conservative evangelical Christian Trump supporter,” is the person who created a crowdfunding effort for Sey and his family. In past commentary, Berry has called for a moratorium on U.S. immigration; stated that “if we’re going to save America, it won’t be enough to deport all the migrants”; and argued that “there’s no such thing as an ‘illegal immigrant with no criminal record’ because illegal immigration is a crime.” He once asserted that “the only due process owed to an illegal alien is deportation.” The crowdfunding appeal he launched states of Sey: “His wife is working to get him released on bail so he can fix any clerical issues that need to be addressed for his legal residence. We are raising money to help his wife and children with expenses while he’s out of work, as well as any legal fees they incur.” It concludes, “Samuel is a good man and a brother in Christ, and his ministry at SlowToWrite has been a blessing to many. Please consider helping. Thank you for standing with them!”

Many in the MAGA coalition criticized Berry for standing with someone they believe to be a lawbreaker. In response, Berry stated both that “Samuel Sey is in my tribe, and he is my brother. And he would make an excellent American,” and that “I of course believe the law should be enforced no matter who it involves.” The due process that Berry has previously dismissed is exactly what could determine whether his friend was arrested because of a clerical error or because he was in fact here unlawfully.

The debate has altered Berry’s perception of his coalition’s moral character. “This has been probably the darkest 24 hours I’ve ever experienced on social media,” he wrote. “The things being said about Samuel, his wife, and his small children are unthinkably evil. There is a segment of the so-called ‘Christian’ nationalist crowd that has given itself completely over to Satan. I’ve never had more resolve to defeat these subversive demons invading the Right and invading Christianity.”

Allie Beth Stuckey, a Christian conservative podcaster for Blaze Media and the author of Toxic Empathy: How Progressives Exploit Christian Compassion, has criticized what she sees as “toxic empathy” in the immigration debate. People are “so focused on the hard journey of the migrant that it belittles the effect of the chaos of illegal immigration on children, innocent citizens, and victims of illegal immigrant crime,” she wrote. In her telling, “Being so empathetic toward one set of people that you’re blinded to everyone and everything else isn’t just misguided, it’s evil.”

But in Sey’s case, she urged her followers to understand and connect with his family’s feelings and perspective. “As you can imagine, his wife, who’s at home with their 3 babies, is devastated and also trusting the Lord to help them find a resolution quickly,” she wrote. “Please pray for all of the Seys.”

Megan Basham of The Daily Wire, who is also a conservative Christian, posted this after learning that Sey had been detained: “I have spoken to people close to my friend Sam Sey, and this is not a question of any deliberate law breaking. Anyone saying otherwise is not telling you the truth. And anyone rejoicing over his and his precious wife Annie’s difficulties in this situation is disgusting.”

I was struck by the contrast with a social-media exchange I had with Basham earlier this month, when I was critiquing the Trump administration for deporting dozens of Venezuelan men to a brutally abusive prison in El Salvador. She was defending it. “Should overstaying your visa in the United States carry the risk of being beaten and sexually assaulted by sadistic prison guards in a foreign dictatorship where you’ve never set foot, paid for by the US government?” I asked her, adding, “I don’t think it should carry that risk. I don’t think Jesus would think it should carry that risk either.”

She replied, “Yes, because you should go home when your visa expires. That’s how Visa’s work. If you don’t, you’re breaking the law and you run the risk of whatever penalties come along with that.”

Some commentators in the MAGA coalition seem to adopt rhetoric and positions on illegal immigration that they can maintain only when they think of illegal immigrants as an abstract “them.” When they confront one who is a concrete “us,” their rhetoric shifts significantly. They raise rather than ignore the possibility of procedural errors, extoll the value of due process, note personal circumstances, draw attention to the suffering of family members, and urge empathy rather than vilification.

Others in the MAGA coalition object to this shift. Some are bigots who use racial slurs in their posts or attack interracial couples such as Sey and his wife. Others are restrictionists who believe that mass deportations are necessary and will cease if illegal immigrants are humanized and shown empathy. I wonder how many of those attacking Sey and his humanizers are those who are triggered by the simple cognitive dissonance of hearing good things about a person who may belong to categories such as “illegal alien” or “lawbreaker”—categories that they are accustomed to coding as evil.

Many in the MAGA movement hope that uncompromising harshness toward all undocumented immigrants will result in maximizing the number of people whom the country is able to deport. But the longer that the mass deportation of otherwise law-abiding people persists, the harder it will be to maintain support for that approach: Rather than assume that deportees are mostly villains, more and more people will have personal connections to productive members of society who got deported.

Certain questions follow. Why does immigration law require someone who marries an American to spend years filling out onerous paperwork with catastrophic penalties for errors? Wouldn’t Americans benefit if the law drew more distinctions between, for example, a visa overstay by a gainfully employed, noncriminal father of American children and a serial perpetrator of violence who twice snuck into the country? A movement that genuinely prioritizes the interests of U.S. citizens would have better answers to such questions than Trump, whose approach is deportations first, not “America first.”

title: Flying Across the World to Vote
summary: Photographs and videos by Dana GolanSince the beginning of the Gaza war, a record number of Israelis have left the country. More than 10 percent of the electorate now lives abroad, and the country generally does not allow absentee ballots: Those who want to vote in today’s election, the first since ...
content:
Photographs and videos by Dana Golan

Since the beginning of the Gaza war, a record number of Israelis have left the country. More than 10 percent of the electorate now lives abroad, and the country generally does not allow absentee ballots: Those who want to vote in today’s election, the first since October 7, need to be there in person.

An estimated 67,000 Israeli expats have traveled thousands of miles—and spent thousands of dollars—to return home. Within Israel, the polls suggest a fairly even split between the parties that favor Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and those that oppose him. But most of the expats are expected to support the opposition. The prime minister’s allies reportedly considered restricting airport capacity to limit the number of arrivals. But the flights still came.

Israelis returning from abroad expressed feelings of deep investment in this election and a belief that the outcome will affect them no matter where they live. Many are willing to travel a long way to vote for what they believe will be a better future.

Dana Golan for The Atlantic
Maya Mor Mitrani, a college student and opera singer in Philadelphia, spoke about concern for her father, who has served in the military reserves since October 7. “I just think the situation is really bad,” she said, “and I want to have at least some influence over how the government tries to solve the problems we’re facing right now. So if my influence amounts to just one ballot in the box, that’s what I’ll do.”
Dana Golan for The Atlantic
Jonathan Matkowsky was born in America, but he moved to Israel in 2012. On October 7, he barricaded his children indoors and drove south to help however he could, working as a volunteer driver for off-duty soldiers and civilians for the next four months. He later moved back to the United States. Now he has returned for the election: “It’s a meaningful vote for me because of how much trauma we’ve been through,” he said. Although he considered voting for Gadi Eisenkot because of his support for extending the draft to the ultra-Orthodox, he ultimately decided to vote for Netanyahu. He trusts the prime minister’s wisdom and experience and credits him with keeping Israel safe: “I’m proud of him. I believe in him. I think he’s a hero,” he said.
Dana Golan for The Atlantic
New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport on October 25, 2026
Dana Golan for The Atlantic
A banner that reads “This time, Eisenkot” hangs in Jaffa, Tel Aviv.
Dana Golan for The Atlantic
An organization called Fly&Vote organized expats to fly from New York to Tel Aviv on October 25.
Dana Golan for The Atlantic
Shirily Bar-Or spent years protesting in Israel before moving to Athens last year. “I didn’t give up, exactly. I just needed to breathe. I was running out of air. I hope I’ll be able to breathe again tomorrow.” What she wants, she said, is for “the country to be sane again. I want a government that works for the public good. I want democracy.” To her, this election is pivotal because, she said, what Netanyahu wants “is to destroy us just to save his own skin.”
Dana Golan for The Atlantic
Dan Galezer lives in New York and already had a trip to Israel planned, but he changed his flight to be there on election day. He said that he didn’t know which opposition party to support, but that “I’m just at the stage of saying: Get Bibi out of the seat already. His time is up.” Galezer’s family’s kibbutz was the site of one of the worst massacres on October 7. “Today, even after everything that’s happened,” he said, “I don’t rule out returning.” But whether that will even be possible, he said, may depend on the outcome of the election: “This feels like a breaking point.”
Dana Golan for The Atlantic
Arie Deizer has lived in Bucharest for 30 years and compared Netanyahu to the Hungarian strongman Viktor Orbán. Netanyahu, he said, has “destroyed the country—he’s completely lost it now,” and Deizer hopes he’ll be “thrown out, just like Orbán.” Deizer is voting for the Democrats, in part because unlike many other opposition parties, they have not ruled out working with Arab parties, should they win. “I hope we’ll have an overwhelming majority here—70 seats—so that the Arab parties can’t be ignored.”

Dana Golan for The Atlantic
A sign on the entrance to a shop in Jaffa, Tel Aviv, reads “Jews and Arabs refuse to be enemies.”
Dana Golan for The Atlantic
Shai Sinai hasn’t lived in Israel for 40 years, but he’s come back from Hamburg to vote in every election since Netanyahu came to power. “I was born here, I grew up here, I was educated here, I served in the army here, and my whole family—the family members who are still alive—basically lives here.” Volunteers from Fly&Vote, a nonprofit dedicated to helping expats return for the election, met him and other voters at the airport. So did members of the Democrats, a party Sinai said he will support. He hopes that the government will be replaced, he said, but “to say that I’m expecting it would be too optimistic.”
Dana Golan for The Atlantic
Volunteers and candidates from the Democrats Party came to greet Israelis as they landed in Israel to vote.
Dana Golan for The Atlantic
Election posters at the entrance to a polling station in Tel Aviv include one from Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad party that reads, “We will only fix this together.”

title: Who Said It: Marissa Mayer, or Odysseus?
summary: Late last year, Marissa Mayer was struggling with what felt like an impossible task. Her daughter Marielle was turning 10, and Marielle’s teacher wanted three bullet points summarizing what made her special. Mayer—the former chief executive of Yahoo and a pioneer at Google, where she was the first f...
content:
Late last year, Marissa Mayer was struggling with what felt like an impossible task. Her daughter Marielle was turning 10, and Marielle’s teacher wanted three bullet points summarizing what made her special. Mayer—the former chief executive of Yahoo and a pioneer at Google, where she was the first female engineer—likes cracking a hard problem. But she felt overwhelmed by the range and complexity of potential answers.

So Mayer asked her personal A.I. assistant, Dazzle. Within a few seconds, Dazzle delivered an answer.

“It came back and was like, your daughter is empathetic, creative and an animal lover,” Mayer said. She thought it was perfect.

In an attempt to express the blend of bewilderment and despair brought on by this New York Times anecdote, I have concocted a quiz: Which is it—a question the tech industry wants me to ask AI, or something Odysseus asks upon returning to Ithaca after 20 years of absence?

Tell me, what is my son like?

Who are these people in my house?

Are any of these people my son’s friends?

Are any of these people my friends?

What makes my son smile?

What would make a good gift for my son?

Do I have anything in common with my son?

Would archery be a fun activity to do to impress my family?

Is there a quicker route home I could take next time?

What would be a nifty surprise for my wife?

What activities or items does my wife enjoy?

What activity can I do to bond with my wife and son?

Does my dog recognize me?

Is there something I can feed my elderly dog that will help him live longer?

I am told this is my home, but I don’t recognize any of these people in my house, and I don’t know what they want. I am told this is my life, but all of the intimate things that should be the most familiar feel foreign to me. Suggest a fun activity to distract me from the terrifying sense that I have hollowed out my life with my own hands, and that my absence has filled my house with strangers!

Is Zendaya Athena?

title: The Limits of Trump’s Midterm Trickery
summary: For the first time in modern American history, a sitting president is seeking to wield the force of the state to secure an electoral victory for his party. The Trump administration has attempted to undermine the widespread use of mail-in voting; demanded that states hand over voter rolls; threatened...
content:
For the first time in modern American history, a sitting president is seeking to wield the force of the state to secure an electoral victory for his party. The Trump administration has attempted to undermine the widespread use of mail-in voting; demanded that states hand over voter rolls; threatened to prosecute state and local election officials; refused to rule out the idea of deploying troops or federal agents to polling places; and publicized the dramatic arrests of small numbers of people accused of voting or registering to vote as noncitizens. Many of these efforts have made little headway—either because of the administration’s incompetence, the stubborn lack of factual evidence behind President Trump’s claims of voter fraud, the federal government’s lack of legal authority, or the refusal of courts to go along with Trump’s plans.

But Trump may have a different problem on his hands. Polls show Trump’s approval falling to all-time lows in the weeks before Election Day; the percent of voters happy with his performance has now sunk into the 30s. Democrats, meanwhile, appear likely to retake control of the House of Representatives and maybe even the Senate, which last year seemed well out of reach. The polls could be wrong—and high-profile-polling misses of the Trump era are hard to forget. But if the polling is right, the GOP may be in for what George W. Bush, after a disastrous 2006 midterm, ruefully termed a “thumping.” And a thumping, as opposed to a narrower Democratic victory, could render most efforts to suppress turnout irrelevant, and make it far more difficult to implement any more dramatic effort to rig the results.

To Trump’s endless frustration, elections in America are organized at the state and local level, with little role for the federal government. In a typical midterm year, almost 470 congressional seats are up for grabs across 50 different states. Though a small number of those races are actually competitive, tinkering with the outcome of the votes would still require meddling with a number of different elections, all run differently, in different jurisdictions, under different laws. A strong night for the Democratic Party would make conjuring an ersatz House majority hard for the same reason that a losing sports team is less able to cheat its way to a victory in a blowout. (Even on a very strong night for the Democrats, the Senate may still be quite a close call.)

Tight margins, by contrast, can make an election more vulnerable to efforts to undo the voters’ will. Trump’s attempt to overturn the 2020 presidential election relied in significant part on tight margins in some swing states, sometimes with only 10,000 or 20,000 votes deciding the winner. In Georgia, the president famously pushed Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “find 11,780 votes” to make up his deficit against Joe Biden. As described by both the House January 6 committee’s report and Jack Smith’s indictment of Trump, Trump and his allies used close tallies in swing states, together with the slow counting of mail-in ballots, to engineer doubts over election results and provide Republican members of Congress with the tools to delay the formal counting of the electoral vote on January 6. The attack on the Capitol followed.

The memory of January 6, and the entrenchment of the election-denier movement since 2020, has led to speculation—both anxious and enthused—about the possibility of a comparable attack on election results in 2026. If, once most of the results are in, Democrats seem set to eke out a House majority by just a few seats, perhaps committed Trump allies in positions of power could make trouble in a handful of the closest districts. A local election commissioner, say, could refuse to sign off on a Democrat’s narrow victory, or the Justice Department could execute a warrant to seize ballots and thus delay or upend the counting of votes. This could create chaos on January 3, when the new House gathers for the first time: What happens if the contested seats are enough to deny the should-be-majority party the votes it needs to select a new speaker and take control of the chamber? Although this isn’t a foolproof trick for stealing control of the House, such a play could make things very precarious very quickly.

But the bigger the majority secured by Democrats, the more difficult it would be for Trump to shave that majority down—the more clerks to convince, warrants to secure, and court rulings to dodge, all over the country. “If there is a House majority in either direction that is 20, 30 seats, I think the likelihood of an attempt to engage in some kind of shenanigans around January 3 is way less than if the majority is two or three seats,” Jonathan Diaz of the Campaign Legal Center commented recently on a preelection panel convened at UCLA’s law school.

Other tricks are also less effective when the vote swings heavily in one direction. For example, Trump’s unprecedented push for explicitly partisan off-cycle redistricting may net only a few extra GOP seats rather than the double-digit gains Democratic strategists had once feared.

Political constraints matter too. Any scheme to steal the House for the GOP would depend on the willingness of congressional Republicans to vote in lockstep, with no defectors—something that the current fractious House Republican caucus can barely manage. Already, though, Republicans spooked by Trump’s bad poll numbers have begun distancing themselves from him on the campaign trail as they fight to hold on to their seats. Over the summer, Republican politicians and MAGA-friendly media outlets responded coolly to a rambling address by the president casting doubt on election integrity. If the GOP loses the House, how many Republicans concerned about their own political careers would be actually inclined to adopt the fringe message of an ever more unpopular lame-duck president? (Trump has been notably quiet recently about the possibility of running for an unconstitutional third term.)    

Trump will be hard-pressed to fight against “a clear loss, coupled with the expectation of a clear loss,” Bob Bauer told me. Bauer—a longtime Democratic lawyer who played a central role in the Biden campaign’s fight against Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election—now focuses on bipartisan election-integrity work, alongside Ben Ginsberg, an election lawyer known for his past work representing the Republican Party. In 2020, Bauer said, the additional days required for the presidential race to be called after the polls closed helped fuel Trump’s claims of fraud. But now, broad public dissatisfaction has aligned with dismal polling for the GOP and a growing anticipation among both politicians and the press that Republicans will do poorly. “It would be very difficult in these circumstances, if things turn out that the Democrats do well, for him to suddenly announce that he was denied his landslide by vote rigging,” Bauer told me.

Just because such a scheme would be implausible does not, of course, mean that Trump won’t try it. Last week, the Justice Department filed a bizarre lawsuit seeking to preemptively block Alaska from certifying the results of its Senate race—but only if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses. (“The legal argument is one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen,” wrote the law professor Derek Muller in an analysis of the case.) DOJ also continues to pursue litigation seeking to force California to set aside mail-in ballots to voters whom the federal government claims to have identified as noncitizens. These cases are sloppy, tardy, and almost certainly doomed. But they do have the advantage of helping Trump and his allies build a narrative about the courts blocking Trump’s efforts to ensure a fair election. Likewise, if a Trump-aligned rogue local election official tried to block a Democratic candidate’s victory, whatever he or she concocted as reasoning could provide fuel for election-fraud rumors on the far right, even if the effort—as it likely would—ultimately failed.

In a wave election, some races will still be close. They may just be in different states or districts—mostly, more Republican ones—than in a year with more typical political geography. House seats in deep-red areas across the country may be newly up for grabs. In the Senate, races in Texas and Alaska stand out as potential flash points. “Any close race in the Senate is going to be hotly, hotly contested,” Bauer told me. He pointed to the bitter fight between the Democrat Al Franken and the Republican Norm Coleman over the 2008 Senate election in Minnesota, which took months to resolve and ended with the courts upholding Franken’s 312-vote victory.

In the final weeks before the midterms, election experts have seemed notably calmer than some of the the anxious rhetoric around Trump’s potential subversion of the vote might suggest. Eight experts interviewed by The New York Times (including Bauer) voiced worries about possible upheaval but overall confidence that officials are prepared to protect the integrity of the elections. The nonprofit publication Votebeat likewise surveyed 31 authorities on election administration and found the group to be wary but “cautiously optimistic” that the midterms will go smoothly. If the elections pass without serious disruption, a hefty margin of victory for the Democratic Party could be partly why. But the fact that such a margin may be needed to avoid chaos is itself sobering. In a healthy democracy, the opposition party should not have to win by enormous numbers to ensure victory, and voters should be able to trust that even a close election will be free and fair.

title: The Illusion of ‘Radical Transparency’
summary: One of the curiosities of Donald Trump’s enduring (if perhaps weakening) grip on his supporters is how they praise him as someone who “tells it like it is.” Trump’s gatekeepers have similarly declared this to be “the most transparent administration in history,” pointing to, among other things, Trump...
content:
One of the curiosities of Donald Trump’s enduring (if perhaps weakening) grip on his supporters is how they praise him as someone who “tells it like it is.” Trump’s gatekeepers have similarly declared this to be “the most transparent administration in history,” pointing to, among other things, Trump’s willingness to open his sycophantic Cabinet meetings to live media coverage as proof that nothing is being obscured.

The irony of this, of course, is that Trump has been caught in more obvious lies than any president in history. Yet by making himself so ubiquitous, Trump breeds an illusion of openness. To him, a president’s ultimate power rests in his ability to always be in people’s faces—to become inescapable, if not honestly examined; to impose his own self-serving version of reality whenever he pleases, no matter how outlandish.

I kept thinking about this as I watched You Can See Everything, the blockbuster documentary that has become a source of cultural fascination since it started packing theaters a few weeks ago. This might be my Trump Derangement Syndrome showing, but I couldn’t help but view the film as a classic Trump-era parable.

You Can See Everything chronicles the disgraced Theranos founder, Elizabeth Holmes, and her fiancé, Billy Evans, during their final 34 days together, with their two young children, before Holmes begins an 11-year prison sentence for criminal fraud. In the opening scene, Evans introduces the promise of “radical transparency.” The couple have invited the filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into their beachside rental house near San Diego. In Evans’s telling, the false narrative of Holmes as a scheming con artist has become so entrenched that they might as well raise every curtain, and allow people see her at this most vulnerable and unguarded time. They have nothing to lose and nothing to hide.

[Read: Can Elizabeth Holmes drop the act?]

Like Trump, Holmes and Evans are rich, famous, and secure in their victimhood. No one should have to go through this, as Trump often says (“no one” meaning himself). No messianic entrepreneur either. Holmes’s aura cries out for caretaking, and not just by Evans, who assumes the role aggressively, or deviously. Her voice goes from insistent monotone at the start to plaintive and soft as her banishment approaches. Everything has been taken from her, unfairly.

Like the president, Holmes is adept at playing to reality-TV sensibilities. She seems to have an intuitive sense for when a flash of frustration or vexation can enhance a scene. The camera loves her, even (or especially) when she is melting down. Holmes recognizes the hypnotic effect of her sad, toddlerlike eyes. “It took me a really long time to be okay with letting someone see me cry,” she confides to Fielder, and then sheds a tear on cue.

Holmes operates not so much with words as with complete denial that she has intentionally hurt anyone. At one point, she claims that she’s never told a lie in her life. And how can anyone doubt her? We can see everything, after all, so maybe the problem is ours. That is the power of radical transparency. It can breed confusion in us, the audience, rather than clarity about the subject.

Fielder, who manages to convey a presence that is both empathetic and dubious, keeps suggesting that Evans and Holmes are not on the level. As the story unfolds, their promise of radical transparency unravels. It becomes evident that Evans is restricting access, manipulating facts, and perhaps exploiting what’s left of his partner’s marketable image.

Over the course of the film, Holmes’s responses to Fielder’s inquiries become mushy pleas of ignorance and confusion. If she is guilty of anything, she seems to suggest, it is of allowing herself to be badly misunderstood. She has erred not morally or legally, but in how she’s communicated. Politicians are always doing this too, placing blame not on their own shortcomings but on their (and their staff’s) failure to properly convey the greatness they’ve achieved.

[Idrees Kahloon: Theranos-style fraud has become the norm]

Many of Silicon Valley’s most charismatic entrepreneurs are skilled at creating belief systems, around their products and themselves, as my colleague David Sims wrote in his review of You Can See Everything. Steve Jobs, the Apple co-founder, is considered the virtuoso of this. Holmes fashioned herself a Jobs acolyte. She wore the same black turtlenecks and intense gaze, and modeled her seductive corporate persona after his (notwithstanding that, unlike Theranos, Apple makes products that actually work). Watching leaders—political or corporate—who project total faith in their ability to persuade and inspire can be mesmerizing. They are convinced that just by getting in front of an audience, they can bring viewers around, no matter what they say or what they are selling. Holmes seems to think this too.

Trump has at times taken his own confidence to absurd extremes. Early on in the coronavirus pandemic, he insisted on near-daily press conferences. He had no grasp of the viral menace at hand but seemed to believe that his presence alone could transcend the scary science. He might have made little sense, but he did so with total conviction. And he made himself so relentlessly visible. That had to be reassuring, right?

One of Trump’s superpowers has been his ability to outlast his skeptics. Still, reality shows can become exhausting—whether it’s two terms of Trump or three hours of You Can See Everything. Even the most compelling stories and storytellers can feel overexposed and stale. Customers eventually lose patience. Revelation gives way to repetition. Suspicion creeps in: Is this really everything? Enough already. The audience is ready for the spectacle to end and the sentence to begin.

content:
Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to safety. Is it a deliberate military strategy?

The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.

“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”

title: Sudan paramilitary drone strikes cause mass power cuts in eastern states
summary: Rapid Support Forces strike five power stations in three states controlled by Sudanese armySudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said.The drones hit t...
content:
Rapid Support Forces strike five power stations in three states controlled by Sudanese army

Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said.

The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref and one in White Nile state, “resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states”, the official said on condition of anonymity.

content:
Calculations from the Center for Global Development say spending next year is likely to be £410m less than anticipated

The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year.

Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027.

title: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus

content:
Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda

Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.

The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.
